extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer-science authors (students and professionals) preparing proofs, papers, books, and literate programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear mathematical and computer-science exposition (proofs, formulas, exercises, book text) and for presenting programs/documentation in literate programming (WEB) style. Covers sentence-level style, notation, typesetting, module structure, and book production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place words between adjacent formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid leaving no words between consecutive formulas in text (e.g., the bad example “Add p k times to c.”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert necessary words so the sentence reads naturally and unambiguously; don't let adjacent math symbols create malformed or ambiguous prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to define symbols before you use them (or at least to define them very near where you use them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure readers encounter a symbol's meaning prior to interpreting expressions that contain it; if unavoidable, place a definition immediately adjacent to first use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous sentence openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get hung up on one or two styles of sentences (e.g., repeatedly starting sentences with 'Thus,', 'Consequently,', 'Therefore,').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence structure to avoid monotony. Use parallelism only when it serves a rhetorical point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallelism purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallelism should be used when it is the point of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ parallel structures to highlight parallels; avoid mechanical repetition otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sentences comprehensible left-to-right
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure sentences so the reader can parse them naturally from left to right (e.g., rewrite 'We prove that hgrunti and hsnorti implies hblahi' to 'We prove that the two conditions hgrunti and hsnorti imply hblahi').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place modifiers and conjunctions so they don't momentarily mislead the reader about what is being proved or listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose placement of 'that' for cadence and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: While guidelines exist, the final placement of the word 'that' must be dictated by cadence and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read sentences aloud to judge cadence and to decide whether including or omitting 'that' improves clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of register (e.g., 'shall')
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'shall' is natural for definitions to many mathematical readers but is considered formal by younger members of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words according to the intended audience's expectations for formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Be precise: if you mean 'not nonincreasing,' don't say 'increasing' (the two have different mathematical meanings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sloppy negation/antonym usage; check logical meaning of descriptive terms to prevent inadvertent strengthening or weakening of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mixed tenses on the same subject (e.g., prefer 'We assume now hgrunti, hoping to show a contradiction' to mixing future/present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tense consistent unless there is a clear reason to shift; mixed tenses can be awkward and misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear phrasing for proofs by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ungainly phrases like 'Assume by contradiction that hblahi.' Prefer 'The proof that hblahi is by contradiction' or 'To prove hgrunti, let us assume the opposite and see what happens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phrasing that clearly signals proof strategy without awkward constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversational signposts and transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational tone giving signposts and clearly written transition paragraphs provides pleasant reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide meta-comments or sectioning like 'The operative word is zero' or 'We divide the proof into two parts' to guide the reader's intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep variable/index order consistent in relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving relations, keep the same relative positions for indices/variables (e.g., prefer 'pi < pj' when you've said 'p = (p1, p2, ..., pn) and i < j' and avoid mixing 'i < j and pj < pi').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order i and j consistently to reduce reader cognitive load and improve visualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite and multiple passes
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should rewrite multiple times in different media (longhand, typing, typesetting) because different passes reveal different issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider composing first in pencil/longhand to keep pace with thinking; edit during transcription to improve flow; expect further passes after typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional designers and copy editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not forget the value of professionals (book designers, copy editors) in producing books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers determine page width, fonts, chapter headings, and typographic distinctions; copy editors catch punctuation and stylistic errors that authors miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical numerals from text numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical numerals (e.g., the zero in math) may need a different glyph (Euler's zero with a point) than text numerals; you must distinguish mathematical numerals from English-language numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful in manuscripts and coordinate with designers so numerals used in formulas are typeset differently where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose prepositions/phrasing by ear for flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtle choices like 'all' vs 'all of' or the position of 'only'/'also' should be decided by ear during editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift words like 'only' and 'also' when editing to improve flow; there's often no single 'right' choice—favor cadence and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why before stating significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell readers why a rule or fact is true before stressing its significance, if reading at speed would otherwise leave them puzzled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reorder exposition so that motivation or proof precedes statements of value when appropriate (example: show proof/why, then state general rule and name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward repetitive prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid constructions that repeat prepositions awkwardly (e.g., 'by replacing – – by – –'); choose alternate phrasing like 'by changing – – to – –'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When repetition creates poor rhythm or ambiguity, rephrase to a clearer construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read at speed to check rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Try reading your text at normal reading speed to get a better sense of sentence rhythm than when you wrote it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud or quickly helps detect awkward rhythms, repetitions, and places needing rewording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't display false equations as assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a bad idea to display false equations; the reader's eye may treat them as gospel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must show a false equation for illustration, put it in quotes or explicitly label it as false and explain why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sure pronoun antecedents are clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the antecedent of any pronoun you use is clear; avoid ambiguous 'It is ...' constructions when 'it' could refer to multiple objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences to name the object or rephrase the sentence for clarity (examples given in Before/After).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid page break within displayed formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure you don't have a page break in the middle of a displayed formula; near the end of editing, rework text to move the formula entirely onto one page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, invent a sentence or two to fill space or change formula layout; treat pagination as part of the editing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order proofs to match definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Let proofs follow the same order as the definitions they rely on; handle separate cases in an order consistent with earlier presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the reader's mental model by aligning the ordering of proofs with previously introduced definitions and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct dash and minus glyphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphens, en-dashes, minus signs, and em-dashes are distinct and should not be used interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphen (shortest) for compounds, en-dash for ranges (e.g., 'lines 10–18'), minus sign in formulas (10 − 18 = −8), em-dash for sentence breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread mathematics as well as prose
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofreading you may catch technical errors as well as stylistic errors; think about the mathematics too, not just the prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check limiting processes, domain distinctions, and the precise mathematical meaning (example: revise x → 0 to 'x decreases to 0' when necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: State contrasts explicitly when using 'instead'
rubrics_metrics.description: When you use the word 'instead', be explicit about the contrast so the reader immediately understands what is being referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'x = −1 instead of +1' over 'x = −1 instead' to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use present tense for timeless facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the present tense for facts that remain true; past tense is acceptable for things that turned out to be in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide tense based on whether the fact is considered eternally true or historically situated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless repetition in sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to avoid repeating words in a sentence; use more precise or varied wording to keep prose clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute synonyms where repetition confuses flow (Before/After examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference equations/tables without excessive page numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Give page numbers only for remote references; usually 'Equation 5.14' is sufficient rather than citing a page number every time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cluttering references with page numbers unless the reference is not easily found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose integral/limit notation based on space and be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting limits above and below the integral trades vertical space for horizontal space; choose the form based on formula width and remain consistent throughout a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early on notation conventions for the whole project and stick to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long formulas logically and consider algebraic changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When long formulas don't fit, break the lines at logical points; in some cases the author can change the math (introduce a new symbol) to make formula placement less jarring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should choose line breaks and sometimes alter notation to improve display; understand equals-sign placement rules: break after '=' in embedded formulas, before '=' in displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust sentence punctuation and paragraphing for flow
rubrics_metrics.description: While editing for flow, sentences can be shortened (change semicolons to periods) or lengthened (periods to semicolons); break paragraphs into smaller ones when helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use punctuation and paragraph breaks as tools to control reading speed and emphasis; ensure conjunction-begun sentences remain clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable naming: avoid misleading similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your variable names are not misleading; variable names that are too similar to conceptually unrelated variables can be confusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic renaming tools in editors, and choose descriptive names (e.g., prefer 'caps_range' over 'range' when appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer slashed fractions in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overuse of stacked fractions with a horizontal bar in running text; they can produce tiny numerals (especially in exponents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy editors often convert stacked forms to slashed forms like (1 + x)/y and add parentheses where needed to preserve meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write exercises with extra context and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises have little context, so ambiguity can be especially deadly; a bit of carefully chosen redundancy is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough specification in exercises to remove ambiguity; recognize exercises are hard to translate and to attribute properly under copyright rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit previously published exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright law makes it necessary to give credit to all previously published exercises; crediting sources is generally sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace historical origins where possible; acknowledge sources to help future authors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answers to exercises may use looser rhetorical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Some rhetorical guidelines can be dispensed with in answers: quick, pithy answers and answers that start with a symbol are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor style for answer sections where brevity and directness are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fixed-width/typewriter font for program listings
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs (algorithms) should be presented in fixed-width type; variable-width fonts were unsatisfactory for readable program listings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix typewriter style with roman/bold/italic for clarity; choose fonts that make identifiers and numbers readable and consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present algorithms in human-readable English (not a specific language)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid alienating readers, do not commit to a single programming language for presentation; write algorithms in English and present steps with comments and invariants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number steps and include parenthetical remarks (comments/invariants) to aid understanding and formal reasoning about correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break complex things into parts and explain twice
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct way to explain a complex thing is to break it into parts and explain each part twice (formally and informally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modules that begin with informal explanation and finish with formal code (WEB practice); provide a high-level intuition and a formal specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at the novice to reach experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to write for the absolute novice; if you do, you'll communicate with experts—otherwise you may communicate with nobody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unexplained jargon; authors accustomed to their field often can't tell when a term is jargon to newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module documentation: give informal but clear high-level description
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should contain an informal but clear description of what it actually does; a play-by-play account is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey intuition and high-level function rather than stepwise narration; keep descriptions concise and focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module length: keep modules small
rubrics_metrics.description: Modules should be short and manageable—about a dozen lines of code is suggested as a reasonable length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If modules are too long, split them into smaller pieces reflecting tractable parts of the algorithm or logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carrying obsolete conventions into new styles
rubrics_metrics.description: When you change style (e.g., to WEB), do not carry excess baggage from older conventions that are no longer appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drop redundant or unnecessary notational habits (for example, end {while} comments used for Pascal are unnecessary in WEB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Module naming: use imperatives for actions, descriptors for declarative content
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor imperatives for modules that perform actions (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary') and descriptors for modules that are lists/declarations ('Procedures for sorting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the first letter of a module name; avoid headline-style full capitalization of every word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier conventions: avoid camelCase after lowercase; use underscores
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifiers like 'FindInNewWords' look bad in print; WEB allows short underscores to conjoin words and avoids ugly capitalization sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer underscores or other readable conventions; remember that TANGLE can remove underscores for the compiler if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a consistent narrator voice for program exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to describe program actions as 'we insert the element' or 'it inserts the element' and be consistent; Knuth favors 'we'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consistent voice helps readers conceptualize program behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment variable declarations, even briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: In WEB you can declare variables at any point; it is always a good idea to add some comment when you do so, even if only very cursory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief comments at declaration sites improve readability and maintainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate typography for multiplication and asterisks
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset asterisks tend to appear higher above the line; prefer the × symbol for multiplication and/or use a typewriter-style font for '*' so it is body-centered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the multiplication glyph/font that produces correct visual alignment in your typeset output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group related routines together
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep related routines (e.g., heap routines) together so they can be read as a group while fresh in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In WEB you are not constrained by top-down ordering, so organize modules for reader convenience rather than strict compilation order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format hexadecimal numbers in typewriter font and decimals in normal type
rubrics_metrics.description: Use typewriter type for hexadecimal numbers (e.g., '3F' in typewriter) and leave decimal numbers in normal roman type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention helps the reader visually distinguish number bases and provides a subliminal type-check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent terminology between documentation and code
rubrics_metrics.description: Words used in the documentation should match the words used in the formal program to avoid confusing the reader with multiple terms for the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a glossary or use consistent identifiers and phrasing across prose and code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer putting begins/ends inside called modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Put your begins and ends inside the called modules (i.e., keep structure local) rather than placing them in the calling module; mixing conventions causes bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow one convention consistently to prevent structural errors and subtle bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate error handling into its own modules
rubrics_metrics.description: WEB encourages keeping error handling and user guidance in separate modules so the main procedure concentrates on normal cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a brief 'Check if the data is wrong' reference in the main module pointing to a detailed error-handling module; this keeps focus and improves error-recovery code quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variable names in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is good practice to use italics for the names of variables when they appear in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent typographic treatment of identifiers in comments improves readability and variable recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let module title variables correspond to local parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the variables in the module title correspond to the local parameters in the module itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This correspondence aids clarity and matches the module's interface to its description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical terms accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use technical phrases (e.g., 'tail recursion') accurately and only when they correctly describe the code's behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misusing impressive-sounding technical terms; wrong usage confuses readers and undermines credibility.
